narrator.name: The Atlas narrator

narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The tradition originated in the Johor–Riau and Riau–Lingga sultanates, circulating through dynastic marriages and trade networks.
It was introduced to Pahang in 1811 for a royal wedding and later moved to Terengganu in 1915.
The most significant development occurred under Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah (1920–1942) and Tengku Ampuan Mariam, who formalised the repertoire.
on_screen: Map: Malaysia · Southeast Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically, Malay gamelan was a private court entertainment performed for royal weddings, receptions, and installations.
It served as a symbol of aristocratic prestige and ceremonial refinement.
Today, it functions as a public performing art and a symbol of Malaysian intangible cultural heritage, performed at cultural festivals and institutional events.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance, historically called Joget Gamelan, features female dancers known as budak joget.
It is characterized by highly stylized, refined movements including specific hand gestures and controlled footwork.
Performances were historically held in palace settings and could last from evening until dawn.
Watch for Timang Burung, Topeng.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (QQhMEHRQLOc)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Performed in palace halls (Istana); dancers move in coordinated groups

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble is smaller than Javanese gamelan and consists of metallophones, gongs, drums, and xylophones.
Specific instruments include the keromong (bonang), gambang (xylophone), demung, saron, kenong, and gongs.
Listen for the keromong (bonang), gambang, demung, saron.

A refined percussion ensemble dominated by the bright, metallic ring of saron and keromong, balanced by the woody resonance of the gambang xylophone. The music is structured around rhythmic cycles marked by deep gongs, creating a sophisticated and courtly atmosphere.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear elaborate court costumes and headdresses.
Historical accounts by Frank Swettenham describe the setting as ceremonial palace halls.
The attire was distinct to the Pahang and Terengganu courts, featuring variations in headdress styles that distinguished the repertoire from other regional dance traditions.
on_screen: Image gallery: 8 licensed images with attribution

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Sultan Ahmad Al-Mu’adzam Shah of Pahang, his consort Che Zubedah, and their daughter Tengku Ampuan Mariam.
Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah of Terengganu was a major patron.
Historically known as Gamelan Pahang or Joget Pahang when centered in Pekan.
It is a subclass of the wider Southeast Asian gamelan family and Malay classical music.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Malay gamelan is parent of Javanese Gamelan: Malay gamelan is part of the wider gamelan family originating from Javanese traditions.
Malay gamelan is sibling of Joget: Shares the historical name 'Joget' but is a distinct courtly form compared to the social dance.
